sources.entry: WhatCable - Tells you, in plain English, what each USB-C cable plugged into your Mac can do — speed, power, and e-marker info — from the menu bar.

summary.one_liner: A macOS menu bar app that explains in plain English what each USB-C cable on your Mac can do (speed, power, e-marker data) and why charging may be slow.
keywords: why is my mac charging slowly
summary.what_it_does: Shows, per USB-C port on an Apple Silicon Mac, what is connected and what it can do: a headline status, a charging diagnostic that names the bottleneck (cable, charger, or battery full), and data-speed verdicts for the Mac port, cable, and device. It decodes cable e-marker chips for speed, current rating and vendor, and lists the charger's advertised power profiles with the negotiated one highlighted. It also lists connected devices in a tree (hubs hidden by default), and shows Thunderbolt/USB4 lanes, generation and tunnels. A command-line tool, whatcable, provides the same data as text, JSON, or a live watch stream. The README also describes a paid Pro tier (live power metering, cable history, display and negotiation diagnostics, terminal dashboard) that is not open source.
use_cases: figure out why a USB-C charger is charging slowly
check what a USB-C cable supports (speed, wattage)
see what is plugged into each USB-C port on a Mac
debug Thunderbolt or USB4 link speed through a dock
inspect USB-C power delivery profiles from a terminal
script USB-C port info as JSON
how_to_run: Download WhatCable.zip from the Releases page, unzip, and drag WhatCable.app to /Applications
notable: Reads USB-C port, PD, e-marker and Thunderbolt state from IOKit with no entitlements, private APIs or helper daemons
Cable identification and USB-IF certification lookup use a bundled offline database, with no network lookup
Mid-session fault warnings read port fault counters, catching cable problems that appear only under load
Localised into about 18 languages, and ships a CLI with --json, --watch and --raw flags
Signed and notarised with Developer ID, distributed outside the Mac App Store
caveats: Apple Silicon only, requires macOS 14 (Sonoma) or later; the README says Intel Macs do not expose the USB-C port-controller data it needs
Most USB-C cables under 60 W are unmarked, so e-marker details are often unavailable for them
Some cables only reveal their e-marker once a device is attached at the far end; desktop front USB ports show devices but no cable or power detail
Pro features require a one-time purchase (up to 2 Macs), and the Pro code is not described as open source
